items.item: self-heal and a sync triggered by an unrelated git change are two different mechanisms with overlapping effects: self-heal off does not mean an edit is permanent, because any sync at all applies the whole desired manifest, not just the changed fields — the edit can still be overwritten incidentally, just not by a mechanism that specifically detected and targeted it

at.step: Survives, gets corrected, or something else?

items.item: Flux's gitless direction does not mean Git has become irrelevant to GitOps generally; it is one project's newer option, and Argo CD's own architecture in this topic's main source is still Git-based — the two are shown as separate, real, differently-evolving tools, not as Git being obsolete

at.step: Two real projects, and Git isn't even required

items.item: a resource-level Prune=false annotation and an application-level allow-empty setting solve two different failure modes: the first stops one specific resource from ever being deleted by this mechanism at all, the second stops an accidental total deletion when git momentarily looks empty — a team that only sets one of the two is still exposed to the other

ignoreDifferences only affects what Argo CD treats as in-sync; it does not stop the autoscaler from changing the field, and does not mean Argo CD will apply a different replica count than what's in git on an actual sync — it specifically means Argo CD will sync, not flag this field, as the sync's own documentation about RespectIgnoreDifferences clarifies the subtlety of

External Secrets Operator and SOPS solve different halves of the secrets problem and are not substitutes for each other: ESO keeps the secret value out of git entirely by fetching it live from an external store, while SOPS's encrypted-commit approach keeps a value in git but encrypted, meaning SOPS still needs a KMS/age/PGP key available at decrypt time, which is itself a credential the cluster needs from outside — the same identity-and-secret-store seam this topic ends on

at.step: The seam: identity and secrets

items.item: progressive delivery tools like Argo Rollouts are built for stateless or horizontally-scaled services; nothing in Argo Rollouts' own documentation claims special handling for a job with exactly one running instance holding irreplaceable state, which is exactly why the stream-job contrast in this topic is stated as design reasoning rather than attributed to Argo Rollouts itself

at.step: Why a stream job resists a gradual rollout

items.item: the IaC-vs-GitOps seam is not a technology boundary (both sides can use YAML, both can be in git) but an ownership boundary: IaC changes typically require broader cloud credentials and touch resources outside any one cluster, while GitOps changes are scoped to objects a cluster's own API server can already create — conflating the two tools does not remove this ownership distinction

items.item: Helm's template rendering happening before Argo CD applies anything means a chart's own hooks (pre-install, post-upgrade) are a separate concern from Argo CD's own sync phases and sync waves — a team moving from plain Helm to Argo-CD-managed Helm needs to re-map chart hooks onto Argo CD's own hook model rather than assuming they carry over unchanged

at.out: a Helm-migration detail below this topic's scope

items.item: 'automatic drift correction' being off by default is itself a deliberate default, not an oversight: Argo CD's own self-heal documentation frames unconditional self-heal as risky for multi-source applications specifically, where a change to one source can trigger an autosync that touches resources whose desired state came from a different, unchanged source

declaring staging-to-production promotion as 'a commit' abstracts over a real operational choice this topic doesn't resolve: whether the production overlay tracks a floating reference (same branch, different path) or a pinned one (an explicit commit SHA or tag) changes whether a later staging change can accidentally reach production without a new promotion commit at all
